Livestock cross-breeding diagram. Top left: a black-and-white Friesian dairy cow with a full udder, labelled with icons of a milk can (high milk) and a thermometer with a red cross (poor heat tolerance). Top right: a white humped White Fulani (Bunaji) cow with long lyre-shaped horns and a small udder, with icons of a sun with a check mark (heat tolerant) and a smaller milk can. A multiplication sign between them. Arrow down to a crossbred cow with a small hump and patchy colouring, with both icons: a large milk can and a sun with a check mark.

Two maize plants side by side with their two inbred parents. Left: two short, thin maize plants with small cobs, each labelled as an inbred line (Line A and Line B). A multiplication sign between them and an arrow pointing right to a much taller, sturdy F1 maize plant with two large full cobs.

Comparison of red blood cells. Left panel: several normal red blood cells, round biconcave discs, flowing easily through a capillary. Right panel: several sickle-shaped (crescent) red blood cells mixed with a few normal ones, jammed together and blocking a narrow capillary.

Three-stage diagram of haemolytic disease of the newborn. Stage 1: a pregnant woman labelled Rh− with an Rh+ fetus (red cells drawn with small yellow D antigen markers) in the uterus; a placenta between them. Stage 2: after birth, a few Rh+ red cells shown entering the mother's bloodstream, and the mother's blood now containing Y-shaped anti-D antibodies (purple). Stage 3: a second pregnancy with another Rh+ fetus; purple Y-shaped antibodies crossing the placenta and clumping and bursting the fetus's red cells.

Step-by-step diagram of producing human insulin by recombinant DNA technology, arranged as a cycle from left to right. 1: a human cell with its nucleus and a highlighted short gene segment (orange) on a chromosome. 2: a pair of scissors icon cutting the orange gene out, with small sticky ends shown. 3: a bacterium (rod-shaped, pale green) with a circular plasmid (blue ring) and a main chromosome; the plasmid is removed and cut open by scissors. 4: the orange gene being inserted into the open blue plasmid, with a small glue-drop icon for ligase, forming a recombinant plasmid (blue ring with an orange segment). 5: the recombinant plasmid entering a new bacterium. 6: many bacteria multiplying inside a large steel fermenter tank with a stirrer. 7: a vial of insulin and a syringe.

Diagram of how Bt crops work. Left: a rod-shaped bacterium labelled Bacillus thuringiensis with a highlighted gene segment. Arrow to a cowpea plant whose cells now contain the gene, shown as a small inset of a leaf cell nucleus with the inserted segment. Right: a caterpillar (pod borer) eating a pod, then shown lying dead, while a bee and a ladybird nearby are unharmed.

Diagram of somatic gene therapy using the patient's own blood stem cells, arranged as a loop. 1: a patient lying on a couch with a tube drawing blood (bone marrow stem cells) from the arm. 2: a laboratory dish of stem cells. 3: a harmless virus particle (hexagonal head) carrying a short highlighted normal gene, attaching to and entering a stem cell, the gene shown entering the nucleus. 4: corrected stem cells multiplying in a dish. 5: the corrected cells being returned by drip into the same patient. 6: inset of healthy round red blood cells made by the corrected cells.

A flow chart of a plant breeding programme in seven boxes connected by arrows, top to bottom. Box 1: two parent cowpea plants, one with many pods (high yield) and one with a shield icon (pest resistant). Box 2: a gloved hand removing stamens from a flower with tweezers and then dusting pollen onto the stigma with a brush; a small paper bag over a flower. Box 3: F1 plants. Box 4: F2 plants showing variety (some tall, some short, some with many pods, some damaged by insects). Box 5: a hand selecting the best plants with check marks. Box 6: field trial plots in rows. Box 7: a seed bag with a new variety tag being handed to a farmer.
